text_fidelity_a:
Hot Wheels 20-Pack of 1:64 Scale Toy Sports & Race Cars, Collectible Vehicles (Styles May Vary) It might seem as if 20 cars is too much at once. Nope! It is wonderful.

Days as a five year-old were best filled with playing in complete abandon. The freedom proffered by youth needed only a few toys to complete the ever-present joy. A few toys which mattered included several tattered but friendly books, a truck or two, an odd shovel and bucket, and, the coup de grace, a Hot Wheels car. Mattel makes a track as well, but a well-made car could take a boy places. This set of 20 is what kindergartners drool over.

A boy has everything in this set: vehicles of all colors, a few truck varieties, some funny looking cars. There are plenty, and frankly, since a few will invariably wind up lost under the couch, eaten by the dog, and buried with other treasures in the garden, having 20 quickly becomes justified.

Why a Hot Wheels car? Because they are made with hard steel. They are painted with a slick color. They hold up to frequent tastings, sand grindings, dirt smearings and other nonsense that comes with power racing in a sandbox. Sticky chocolate wipes off with warm water, and grime comes out with a good spray under the faucet.

The wheels themselves have a bounce peculiar to a genuine Hot Wheels vehicle. That's how my brother and I made sure it had adequate fuel. Ten bounces should be enough, we figured, and usually, we were right.

I fully recommend the "Hot Wheels 20-Car Gift Pack."

Anthony Trendl
AmericanSpeechwriter.com
text_fidelity_b: Hot Wheels 20-Pack of 1:64 Scale Toy Sports & Race Cars, Collectible Vehicles (Styles May Vary)

Overall this is a cute game, and it's nice that it has some physical activity in it. They aren't just sitting down for it. One kid who does it continuously can get quite a workout. My kids enjoyed it. I think it would also be nice for a party.

Contained inside is one Fortnite figure and the base that the figure and globe rest on is the actual vehicle itself. Fortnite fans have any number of toys they can buy that feature their favorite Fortnite characters, but the Fortnite Baller Vehicle is one of the cooler ones available. The remote-controlled movement sets this toy apart and it’s a great choice for fans of these action figures.

Brickyard Building Blocks 177 Pieces Large Building Block Toys for Children Ages 1.5-5, Bulk Block Set, Compatible with Duplo (177 pcs) We like the Lego brand, but sometimes we need a lot of bricks without paying an exorbitant amount of money. The 1,100 piece kit from Building Bricks was exactly what we were looking for. The Big Questions:
1. Do they really work well with Lego Brand Legos?
Yes - they work very well. It's difficult to tell the difference if you're not really trying hard.
2. How much cheaper are they? Is it really worth it?
It's hard to compare exact pricing here because this set does not include wheels, doors or special pieces. If I had to choose a product to compare it to, I'd probably compare it with Lego's XXL Classic Box (https://www.amazon.com/10697-Building-Large-Creator-Pieces/dp/B00XJ5C4FW). When pricing per piece, the Lego box is about 5¢ per piece. And yes, you read that right. You're dolling out a nickel for every piece of plastic with Lego's brand stamped on it. :) Building Bricks runs about 3¢ per piece. So the answer is: It's almost half the price - very worth it if you're just needing a lot of standard pieces.
As a side note: We really liked the color choices Building Bricks made. They're perfect for expanding your Lego creation palette.
text_fidelity_b: Brickyard Building Blocks 177 Pieces Large Building Block Toys for Children Ages 1.5-5, Bulk Block Set, Compatible with Duplo (177 pcs)

text_fidelity_a:
Thames & Kosmos Ooze Labs: Alien Slime Lab Science Experiment Kit & Lab Setup, 10 Experiments with Slime | A Parents' Choice Recommended Award Winner This is a pretty expensive science kit given what you're going to make - 4 very small batches of slime and a few "experiments" to go with it - but the value of the product is in the education your children will receive from doing it. Most slime kits are "here's the ingredients, now mix and play". This one gives you the ingredients, tells you to mix, and then gives you a "scalpel" and tells you to go to work.

This is a safe kit that is fine for the age range indicated on the box, although young scientists are probably going to need assistance from Mom and Dad on a few experiements, because a few of them are tricky given the limited space in the instructon manual.

You're going to need to head to the store as well, so be prepared that not everything you'll need is in the box. Some items are very common, others are a bit more unusual.

Overall, this was our favorite slime kit, and a great learning tool.

text_fidelity_a:
Akedo Ultimate Arcade Warriors Ultimate Battle Arena Action Figure, 3 Pieces This retails for about $30. At that price I think it's a great little toy and highly giftable. For whatever reason the price is crazy high on Amazon at the time of this review (about double the retail price). It is not worth nearly $70. That is just crazy.

Going with the retail value, I will review it as a $30 toy.

It does feel a bit flimsy with how the pieces snap in and out of the arena. You may need to help younger kids, and it's best if you really do try to line up the teenie tiny triangle on each piece with the triangle printed on the arena piece. Makes it much easier to snap your fighter in. Also, make sure you cut off the plastic rubber band harnessed around each fighter. Otherwise they are invincible, that was a fun discovery when kiddo went undefeated and we realized it was because his guy couldn't die.

Speaking of kiddo, my son is 9 and LOVES this thing. I was bored in about 10min, but I'm guessing mid-40s mom is not the target demographic. My husband had a bit more fun, and those two really got crazy with it. There does seem to be some technique involved, past just smashing into each other until someone wins. But hey, its how I played Street Fighter back in the 80s, and mashing all the buttons is how I play Akedo in 2021.

Also, the numbers on the pieces for offense and defense are pointless. Some fighters are just better, there isn't any way around it. The defensive pieces usually just mean you will never land an attack and are pointless.

TL;DR: for the $30 the kid loves it. I could see this being a popular birthday party gift.
text_fidelity_b: Akedo Ultimate Arcade Warriors Ultimate Battle Arena Action Figure, 3 Pieces

text_fidelity_a: Disney Colorbrain, The Ultimate Board Game for Families who Love Disney This game is harder than you might think. I thought my Disney knowledge was pretty good, but I was stumped on maybe 1/3 of the questions during the two games I played. My younger Disneyphiles did about the same as me. You might remember that the caterpillar in Alice in Wonderland is blue, but can you recall the color of the flags that sit atop the hats of the Tweedles? There are some questions that require you to come up with as many as five different colors, all of which must be correct for you to gain a point. What color is Celia's dress from Monsters Inc? What three colors are seen in Go Go Tomago's superhero suit from Big Hero 6?  You need to answer quickly, by putting down your selected color cards in front of you. This is actually pretty fun and interesting. Minor characters can be especially tricky. There were a few cards with answers that we disagreed with, such as the one that said Joy from Inside Out wore a yellow dress, when we all see it as green. The answer cards all have pictures from the animated films, and sometimes the photo is not great quality. My family enjoyed this game despite these issues and found it a more challenging activity than we had anticipated. It takes almost no time to learn how to set up and play. You can fill ten minutes or half an hour easily.
text_fidelity_b: Disney Colorbrain, The Ultimate Board Game for Families who Love Disney

SmartLab Toys Demolition Lab: Wrecking Ball Kids are destructive little monsters. Not all the time, and let's face it, not just kids. This toy caters to that inner monster that just likes to see the world burn in anarchy...but on a small not scary scale.

This is pretty much what you would expect: take plenty of time to build something. Make it big and tall. Take a heavier thing and destroy it. Relish your god-like status as you stare into the ruins, maybe making some sound effects that result in spraying saliva all over the sad wreckage.

As an adult, it might be harder to see the appeal or imagine it as anything so big or exciting, but kids can really get into their imaginations and visualize a much larger and complicated version of what is actually happening, which to us, is some cardboard flats falling down. Sometimes simple is pretty effective, and while the value of the toy isn't huge (kind of expensive for build and break cardboard, basically), it really is effective!
text_fidelity_b: SmartLab Toys Demolition Lab: Wrecking Ball

Really, this is a generic puzzle game in which you race to build a complex shape from a card based on a set of pieces each player has. The pieces are made up of squares that look like a disassembled cube, but it could just as easily be Tetris-branded, Lego branded, or any other shape that one might associate with a popular name. You see they have to view an app, which shows a speedometer. They need to keep the needle at a certain speed. Speedometer graphics is broken down into 2 colors, blue and red. If you go to the red, chances are good your car will fly off the tracks. How do you control the speed? By pumping the booster. The faster you pump, the needle will move towards the red. So you need to time yourself and not pump too slow, or too fast to keep the needle in the blue at all times. My kids seem to think it's fun, so that's all that matters. We had been experimenting with kit electric motors, magnets and radios and everything ended up mixed in a box that he liked to play with, so there was interest in this type of toy.

The parts of this kit snap together on a clear plastic grid. The instruction book is a black and white center stapled pamphlet that can be challenging to decipher for builds that are more complex. The kit seems durable but not indestructable. My kids can be pretty rough on things so they have been using this kit with my supervision.

For most kids under 10, this is not the type of toy that they can play with on their own. I have my son use this toy at the dining room table. We check to make sure that all of the parts get back in their place when we are done.

This is an educational toy. My experience is that early exposure to learning experiences like this can shape interests later on in life.

I would have liked to have seen a description of what the various modules do to the electricity to make the magic happen.

text_fidelity_a:
ETA hand2mind Connecting People, Set of 96 This educational toy consists of small, easily swallowed pieces, making it a choking hazard. Thus, it is not recommended for children younger than age 5 and should be kept well away from pets, especially puppies who like to chew things. This toy is recommended for grades K-4, which is approximately ages 5-9. It's primary purpose is helping children learn counting. They can also use it to learn to sort and classify.

The set includes 96 pieces of sturdy, plastic, free-standing, girl and boy figures. Half are male and half female. The pieces come in three sizes, each in four colors, yellow, red, green and blue. The sizes are all rather small, ranging from only 1/2 inch to 1 inch in height. The larger figures weigh about 3-4 grams and the smallest figures weigh about 1 gram. The figures are well made in terms of having smooth surfaces, which is important to avoid harming small fingers. The figures are stored in a zip-lock type plastic bag.

As advertised, the pieces do stand up by themselves, and they can be linked together. However, it can be difficult for younger children to clip them together. They each have a protruding peg on one hand and a hole on the other hand. It takes hand-eye coordination to match up a peg and a hole, and some finger strength to shove a peg into a hole. Taking them apart is even harder. Thus, this toy can be frustrating to kids on the younger end of the recommended age range, 5-6 years old, and is most likely to be handled smoothly by children on the higher end of the scale, age 7-9. LEGO Classic Bricks and Houses 11008 Kids’ Building Toy Starter Set with Fun Builds to Stimulate Young Minds (270 Pieces) The Lego Classic Bricks and Houses set is more open ended than themed sets. The included instructions give steps for a small house, a castle, an igloo, a windmill, a family home, and a lighthouse. You can build all of these at the same time, without having to deconstruct anything.

This set reminded me of when I was a kid, taking out my bucket of Legos and just building whatever came to mind, instead of following the instructions to a specific set.

This set includes a good assortment of colors and pieces, and hopefully the different building techniques and different house styles will inspire kids to try out their own house, or whatever else they want to build. That’s the aim of the Lego Classic line, to inspire kids to make their own creations, and I think the pieces here are good for that.

It could make a good gift for the beginning Lego builder, especially if you’re unsure of what theme they might prefer, or be a good complement to other Lego Classic sets.

Hasbro Gaming Battleship Shots We've only had this a few days so far, but my kids love it so far! They and their neighborhood friends were playing almost non-stop this entire weekend. It's a pretty unique concept and not at all what I expected coming from the original battleship: Rather than the game of strategy (and sometimes just luck!) that the traditional battleship is, this is mostly a game of skill. There is still some strategy in how you align your boats, but rather than try to determine where the other player's position is, you can see their board and have to toss one of the included ping-pong balls into the holes. Land a ball in all the boat's places, and you've sunk their ship! It is definitely reminiscent of beer pong in skillset, or perhaps one of those arcade games that require you to land a ball in a colored cup. You definitely need more space to play since there will be balls bouncing around if/when you miss, but it is a lot of fun. A creative twist on a classic game!
One thing that is a little strange to me however, is the advertising. The listing for this product says "Nostalgic tabletop gameplay meets interactive digital content for an immersive gaming experience". There's nothing digital about this, let alone interactive digital and immersive. It's a pretty fun analog pick-up-and-play game, which is what I like about it actually, but it was hard to determine what we were getting before we tried it.
text_fidelity_b: Hasbro Gaming Battleship Shots

Pop Up Super Mario Family and Preschool Kids Board Game, 2-4 Players, Suitable for Boys & Girls Ages 4+ If you, like me, are looking for games to play with a high energy, lack of focus little boy, then this is the game for you. For my four year old, games with a lot of rules and that require skills he's still learning with clear winners and losers are not the best choice games for us. He doesn't have the patience, skill, or temperament. I needed games to slowly introduce him into those skills and Pop Up Pirate is that game! The only rule, everyone takes turns to place a sword into a slot. The person who makes the pirate pop-up out of the barrel wins. We don't play winner/loser, but you can if you choose to do so.

The game comes with 20 swords, four colors with five each, a barrel, and said pirate. It's for 2 to 4 players, my son and I just pick up a sword no matter the color, but if you have more kids or players, then you can choose colors. You stick the pirate in the barrel where there is a trap/spring mechanism that is only triggered when someone sticks a sword in the right slot. Each player takes a color and everyone takes turns sticking a sword into a slot. When the right sword pokes the pirate, he pops high up into the air. The pirate is fairly light weight so if he were to really go flying he would not break anything or hurt anyone. The pirate jumps at most 2 feet into the air, probably less. The only caveat is to make kids aren't sticking their face near the barrel with the pirate in the hole for obvious reasons. This game comes in fairly big box as the barrel is about as wide as a clothes iron, but not nearly as tall.

If you need a game for toddlers/preschoolers that is guaranteed to teach taking turns and highly giggle inducing, then Pop up Pirate is your game!
text_fidelity_b: Pop Up Super Mario Family and Preschool Kids Board Game, 2-4 Players, Suitable for Boys & Girls Ages 4+

Seems to run maybe 20 minutes or so on a fill and you get about 4 fills from a bottle of the 2 liter Gazillion Bubbles solution. It can make a but of a mess on the ground under the machine so be sure to place it somewhere that doesn't matter or is easy to clean. I didn't find the machine all that difficult to clean after using but you have to have a little patience. Hold it upside down and use the garden hose on low flow to wash out the solution tray being careful not to wet the motor or switch.. We ran this off and on over the 3 day July 4th weekend and it ran perfectly. Kids and adults both were amazed. If you want a bubble machine and don't want to spend a lot of money get this one.

This is one of those interesting ones I couldn't really understand until we got it. The car is sort of on an "assisted loop", in that there are points that require your intervention to continue. It starts off being "spit out" by the dragon, then fired from a booth, then launched up a loop, and- if everything goes according to plan - it lands on the head of the dragon which will either fall forward or to the side (not knowing which way is part of the fun). However, if you don't have everything 100% seated properly, it just fails miserably. My kids had trouble getting it to work until I came and reseated some parts more forcefully, but even then we still had a few misfires that caused it not to work.
But I suppose that's the tradeoff of the more obscure track sets, sometimes they are more difficult to operate successfully. Part of the fun is making it work, I think. But if you have a kid who isn't up for that challenge, maybe this isn't the set for them. We actually really liked it, and the payoff when it DOES work is the sort of moment that gets high fives and cheers all around.
